DEVELOPMENT

Ask about software access before the robot arrives.

The difference between a demonstration mode, an SDK, and the development permissions your project needs.

H
HUMANOID EditorialResearch, hardware & practical perspectives
EDITORIAL DATE3 Aug 20264 min read

AI-generated editorial concept visualization; fictional unbranded hardware.

IN THIS STORY

THE KEY IDEA

Treat software access as part of the purchased configuration, not an assumption attached to the model name.

A robot can be programmable in one sense and restricted in another. A supported high-level application interface may be enough for one team, while another requires access to sensors, joint commands, or a simulation model. “Has an SDK” is the beginning of an evaluation, not the conclusion.

01

Write the interfaces your project requires

List the information you need to read and the behaviors you need to control. Include update rates only where they matter to the application. A clear interface list is easier for a supplier to answer than a broad request for full access. Ask for documentation that maps to the exact edition.

02

Distinguish examples from permissions

An example project shows a supported workflow. It does not necessarily establish what you can modify, redistribute, or deploy commercially. Review the relevant software terms and ask the supplier to resolve ambiguities. Keep any promised access in the quote or written configuration description.

03

Look at setup and recovery

Find out how the environment is installed, how versions are managed, and how a failed update is handled. Ask which parts depend on external services. Good recovery documentation matters because development inevitably involves changing software, not simply running the first example successfully.

04

Evaluate with the team that will use it

Have the intended engineers read a real API example and trace one task from command to observation. Record unclear dependencies. This small exercise can reveal integration questions while they are still inexpensive to resolve, before shipping dates and hardware commitments limit the available choices.

05

Trace one experiment through the interface

Choose a small proposed experiment and describe its complete path through the software. For example, the team may want to request a supported motion, read the resulting state, save observations, and repeat the sequence with one changed parameter. Ask which documented interfaces support each step and which configuration includes them. Identify any external computer, account, service, or optional software package required. This exercise is more revealing than collecting a list of programming languages. It connects software access to a real result the team wants to produce and gives the supplier a precise set of questions to resolve before purchase.

06

Separate the development environment from the robot configuration

Record both the software installed on the developer's computer and the software configuration on the platform. Include versions, supported operating environments, and the installation instructions used. Ask how those two sides are kept compatible when one changes. A team can lose time diagnosing an apparent hardware issue that actually follows from an undocumented environment change. Preserve the first working setup and reproduce it on another suitable machine before heavily modifying the project. The goal is a repeatable development process. A successful example that depends on one unrecorded laptop configuration is a useful first step, but it is a fragile foundation for shared research or long-term maintenance.

07

Ask how experiments leave useful records

Before the first trial, decide what information must be saved to understand a result. That might include commands issued, timestamps, reported state, application messages, configuration, and the software revision. Confirm which observations are actually available through the purchased interface. Choose a simple recording format that the team can inspect after the experiment and keep it with the conditions of the run. Do not promise analyses that rely on signals the platform does not expose. A well-documented small record is more valuable than a large collection of unexplained files. It also makes a support request clearer because the supplier can see what the team requested and observed.

08

Evaluate ownership after the first developer leaves

A software purchase decision should account for the person who will maintain the project next year. Ask where installation instructions, credentials where applicable, source files, and configuration records will be stored under the organization's normal practices. Assign responsibility for updates and for reviewing changes to the supported environment. Establish how a new team member can reproduce a documented example without borrowing a previous developer's personal setup. Where licenses or service access matter, have the appropriate person review the actual terms for the intended use. These steps turn software access into an operational capability that belongs to the team, instead of a collection of permissions and habits understood by only one developer.

MAKE IT PRACTICAL

Your next step.

  • Define required read and control interfaces.
  • Confirm development rights for the exact edition.
  • Review setup, versioning, and recovery documentation.
